catalog_citation: Schebesta, Paul. 1952. Les Pygmées du Congo belge. Mémoires de l'Institut Royal Colonial Belge, Section des sciences morales et politiques, T. XXVI, fasc. 2. Bruxelles: IRCB. 441 pp. Chapter 'Langage des Pygmées' (pp. 368-401), section I 'Le groupe des langues bira-sua (BS)' (K = kango) and §3 'Phonétique efé et phonétique pygméenne en général'. Tone key p. 377; genitive -a- and contracted-syllable tone p. 383; negation particles with final high tone p. 388; contraction/'accent' p. 393. Open digital copy: KAOW/ARSOM digitised memoirs.

catalog_quote: Signes diacritiques: Ton musical: ' au-dessus de la voyelle [ó; scan '6']: ton haut. - au-dessus de la voyelle [ō; scan '5'], n'est jamais signe d'allongement, mais le signe du ton chanté, plus élevé que le ton parlé. " au-dessus de la voyelle [ő; scan 'i']: ton haut ascendant (montant depuis le ton chanté). ˇ au-dessus de voyelle [ǒ; scan 'u']: ton retombant (descendant depuis le ton chanté). [p. 377; all four example vowels are o in] ... Il semble toutefois qu'en pareil cas, la particule -a- ait été absorbée par contraction, ce qu'indique le ton haut ascendant de la syllabe contracte. [p. 383, after K. and S. genitive examples: K. sokǎ mo < soka á mo] ... (e) pá, (e) pí, (e) bi, avec ton haut sur la syllabe finale. K. kango epí, Pl. bakango bepí, Kango n'est pas là. [p. 388] ... L'élision et la contraction des consonnes et des voyelles laissent des traces dans la hauteur du ton musical: S: bu < büi = il a saisi; ce phénomène suit ses lois propres. ... En SK, conformément à la position du génitif dans ces langues (génitif postposé), c'est le contraire qui se produit. La voyelle initiale de la seconde racine se maintient et conserve l'accent. Mais en fait, c'est la même règle qui joue dans les deux cas: l'avantage est donné au déterminé. [p. 393]

new_statements.translation: Musical tone: ' over the vowel: high tone. ¯ over the vowel is never a length mark but the mark of the sung tone, higher than the spoken tone; ˝ over the vowel: high rising tone (rising from the sung tone); ` over the vowel: falling tone (falling from the sung tone). ... Elision and contraction of consonants and vowels leave traces in the height of the musical tone [...] In S K [sua, kango], in keeping with the position of the genitive in these languages (postposed genitive), the opposite happens: the initial vowel of the second root is kept and keeps the accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is stated. Schebesta transcribes kango (and sua, bira, efé) with lexical/grammatical musical tone (high, 'sung', high-rising, falling) and uses 'accent' only to say which vowel survives, with its prominence, when two words contract in sua-kango genitive compounds (the initial vowel of the second, head root). Nothing is said about a fixed or predictable stress position in the word.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the analysis is explicitly provisional ('compte rendu provisoire'), based on 1930/1935/1949-50 field notes, and a fuller volume on the Ituri languages was announced but not found in the KAOW list.
new_statements.domain_note: Transcription conventions for isolated words and short sentences elicited from Bakango/Basua informants (often via Bantu interpreters, which Schebesta says masks pygmy peculiarities); the 'accent' remark concerns word-internal contraction in genitive phrases, not citation-form word stress. The closest modern statement is for Bila, of which Kango is treated as a dialect: three tones H, L, xL + downstep (Kutsch Lojenga 2003 §2.3), silent on stress; Kutsch Lojenga says Kango lexical data 'have not been fully analysed'.
new_statements.identity_note: kzy 'Kango (Tshopo District)' = the Bakango (also Bango, Batchua/Kibatchua, Basua) Mbuti pygmies of the Apare river between Bafwasende and Bomili, who live among the Bali (bcp, D21) and Ndaka and speak Bali as a second language. Schebesta 1952 (pp. 370-372) calls their camp language 'le pur dialecte sua' within his 'bira-sua' group (K = kango, S = sua, B = bira); Bahuchet 2006 (pp. 13, 32) makes Kango the southern dialect of Sua = Bila (Bantu D30); Wikipedia/Ethnologue 18 list kzy as 'Kango–Sua' dialects of Bila (bila1255, D311/D32); Kutsch Lojenga 2003: 450-452 keeps it a separate, unanalysed language 'spoken by a group of pygmies' that 'links the Bali and Komo areas'. Not to be confused with Kango (Bas-Uélé District) kang1286 / Likango (C.50 Ngombe group, Poko). Schebesta's kango data are therefore the right variety for kang1285.

sources.note: No word-stress rule. The diacritics key (p. 372) defines marks for 'ton musical': high tone, 'sung' tone higher than spoken tone, high-rising tone, falling tone; pp. 386-388 'Phonétique efé et phonétique pygméenne' notes glottal stops, labiovelars, and that elision/contraction 'laissent des traces dans la hauteur du ton musical'; in S K (sua-kango) genitive contraction 'la voyelle initiale de la seconde racine se maintient et conserve l'accent'. The word 'accent' otherwise means pronunciation ('un fort accent non négroïde', p. 369). The only 'également accentuées' remark (p. 367) is Stuhlmann…
